intro: Above the Arpaçay gorge, in Kars province, lies an abandoned medieval capital once called the 'city of 1001 churches'. This is Ani, whose story begins in the 5th century AD. Listen closely: these empty streets were once full of life.
history: Ani grew on the Silk Road, and its population is estimated to have approached 100,000. So why is it empty today? Earthquakes struck, trade routes shifted, and in the end the city was abandoned.
structure-1: You are now before Ani Cathedral, the domed basilica the architect Trdat built between 989 and 1001. Its drum and dome fell in the earthquake of 1319. From outside it is a plain rectangle; the arms of its cross show only in the gables of the roofs. A blind arcade of tall arches on slender paired shafts runs round all four sides, and deep triangular niches are cut into the walls. Behind it, picture a stretch of the city's double wall with its round towers.
structure-2: And here is the Menüçehr Mosque, a Seljuk building regarded among the oldest mosques in Anatolia. Within a single city, cathedral and mosque tell the story of Ani's many lives.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the city walls, the Church of the Redeemer and the Maiden's Castle.
facts: Did you know? The Menüçehr Mosque is regarded as the oldest known Seljuk mosque in Anatolia. Ani was known as the city of a thousand and one churches, and at its height it approached a hundred thousand people, spoken of alongside Constantinople and Baghdad. Trdat, the cathedral's architect, was the very man who repaired the earthquake-collapsed dome of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. When the Silk Road shifted, and after the earthquake of 1319, the city emptied. Today it stands on the border, alone in the steppe.
outro: This brings our journey through Ani to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have waited for centuries; let them keep waiting for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
